newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. arms official in Iraq to solve missile engine row.
newsitem.headline: U.N. arms official in Iraq to solve missile engine row.

text.p: Chief U.N. weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus arrived in Baghdad on Sunday to try to persuade Iraq to allow the removal of scrapped missile engines for analysis abroad, a U.N. source said.

Iraq last month prevented a team of U.N. arms inspectors from moving the engines. Ekeus, chairman of the U.N. Special Commission on Iraq, said Baghdad's rejection violated its obligations under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire.
The Security Council last week called on Iraq to cooperate with Ekeus by allowing his experts to remove the engines.
The U.N. source said Ekeus would hold his first meeting with Iraqi officials later on Sunday and would see Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz on Monday. He is scheduled to spend four days in Baghdad.
The missile engines were unearthed by a U.N. arms team. UNSCOM says it needs to analyse them in order to provide an exact accounting of banned Iraqi long-range missiles.
The engines belong to about 80 missiles with ranges beyond the 150 km (90 miles) maximum Iraq is allowed to possess and manufacture under the ceasefire.
About 60 engines are packed in boxes at UNSCOM headquarters in Baghdad. The rest are still buried at sites close to Baghdad.

UNSCOM says it has not yet been able to obtain a clear accounting of Iraq's missiles because it later learned Iraq was capable of producing its own missiles. Ekeus has said between six and 16 missiles are unaccounted for.

Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf said last week Iraq would cooperate fully with Ekeus to close the file on its long- range missiles. He said Iraq was pleased to see more Russian experts working with UNSCOM.

UNSCOM wants to take the engines to the United States for analysis. Iraq says their removal without Iraqi participation would contradict the spirit of an agreement the two sides signed last June after a previous standoff.
Removal of sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait hinges in part on verification by Ekeus that Iraq no longer possesses weapons of mass destruction.

Iraq is expected this week to resume limited exports of oil under a separate deal struck with the United Nations that will allow purchases of humanitarian items to ease the impact of the sanctions on the Iraqi people.
